x.A: Control Tower data residency guardrails can deny access to all Regions except ap-northeast-3 and can deny internet access, so they enforce both rules across accounts.
x.B: AWS WAF filters web requests to resources like ALBs and CloudFront. It cannot stop VPCs from reaching the internet, and there is no account setting for denying Regions that way.
x.C: Service control policies in Organizations can prevent actions that create internet access, such as attaching an internet gateway, and can deny all Regions except ap-northeast-3.
x.D: Per-VPC network ACL rules and per-user IAM policies are manual, hard to keep consistent, and can be changed by administrators, so they are not a reliable guardrail.
x.E: AWS Config rules only detect and alert after a resource is created. They do not prevent it, so the requirement is not enforced.

x.A: Session Manager is for shell access to instances and has nothing to do with starting and stopping an RDS DB instance.
x.B: A cache doesn't remove the database instance cost, and the data could go stale, so it is a poor way to save money.
x.C: Running an EC2 instance with a cron job adds an instance that costs money and has to be managed, so it increases cost.
x.D: Lambda functions start and stop the DB instance, and EventBridge scheduled rules invoke them at the right times. Stopping RDS for the 12 hours when it's not needed saves instance hours.

x.A: Storing everything in Standard-IA from the start charges retrieval fees for the popular, newer files that are accessed frequently.
x.B: Intelligent-Tiering adds a monitoring fee per object, which is expensive for millions of files, and the access pattern is already known by age.
x.C: S3 Inventory only reports on objects. It doesn't move them. A lifecycle policy does that.
x.D: A lifecycle policy moves objects from Standard to Standard-IA after 90 days. The newest, most accessed files remain in Standard, and older infrequently downloaded ones are cheaper. The files are at least 128 KB, so IA's minimum size is not an issue.

x.A: Governance mode lets users with special permissions bypass the lock and delete objects, and a legal hold has no fixed period, so it doesn't meet the one-year rule.
x.B: Compliance mode with a 365 day retention period means no user, including the root user, can modify or delete an object for a year. Scientists can still add new files.
x.C: An IAM role and bucket policy can be changed by administrators, so they don't guarantee files cannot be modified or deleted.
x.D: Tracking hashes with Lambda only detects changes afterward and doesn't prevent modification or deletion.

x.A: DataSync moves data between storage systems and doesn't cache or deliver content to users around the world.
x.B: Global Accelerator can't use S3 buckets as endpoints and doesn't cache content.
x.C: CloudFront caches the media at edge locations around the world and delivers it quickly. It can restrict access to confidential content with signed URLs or cookies.
x.D: SQS is a message queue and does not deliver or cache media files.

x.A: Athena runs one-time SQL queries directly on data in S3 with no infrastructure, and QuickSight builds KPI dashboards from the results, so both are serverless.
x.B: Kinesis Data Analytics processes streaming data. It is not meant for one-time queries on data staged in S3.
x.C: Custom Lambda functions moving individual records to Redshift is a lot of code and cluster management.
x.D: Loading data into multiple OpenSearch clusters adds cost and management work, and OpenSearch is a search engine, not the right staging for BI queries.
x.E: Lake Formation blueprints and Glue can ingest batch data and load it into S3 in Parquet format with little custom work, which fits staging in S3 buckets.

x.A: A manual snapshot is kept until deleted, but it needs someone to take it and delete it manually after 5 years, so it isn't the most automated approach and doesn't cover the audit logs.
x.B: Automated backups have no lifecycle policy feature you can configure that way.
x.C: Aurora automated backup retention is limited to 35 days, so it can't be set to 5 years.
x.D: Exporting the database's audit logs to CloudWatch Logs keeps them, and the retention can be set to never expire, so the audit logs are kept indefinitely.
x.E: AWS Backup can take scheduled backups of Aurora and keep them for 5 years, then delete them automatically.

x.A: CloudFront delivers both live streaming and on-demand video from edge locations around the world, improving performance for a global audience.
x.B: Global Accelerator improves network path performance for TCP and UDP applications, but it doesn't cache on-demand video at the edge.
x.C: Route 53 is DNS and doesn't deliver or accelerate content.
x.D: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads to S3 and doesn't improve live streaming to viewers.

x.A: A usage plan with an API key shared only with genuine users gives you a way to identify and throttle callers. Requests without a valid key are rejected.
x.B: Handling fraudulent IP addresses in Lambda means the function still runs and costs money for each request, and a botnet uses many changing IPs.
x.C: AWS WAF rules can filter malicious requests before they reach the API, for example by blocking known bad IPs or rate limiting.
x.D: A private API is reachable only from a VPC, so genuine public users could no longer use it, which defeats the purpose.
x.E: Creating an IAM role for every user is not scalable for a public API.

x.A: OpenSearch Service is a costly cluster for just 300 MB per month and is not a backup store.
x.B: Glacier retrieval takes minutes to hours, so data would not be available in milliseconds.
x.C: S3 Standard gives millisecond access at a low price, and 300 MB a month is very small, so the cost is minimal. The data can be deleted after 30 days with a lifecycle rule.
x.D: RDS for PostgreSQL runs an instance continuously, which costs far more than S3 for backup storage.

x.A: Running the code on multiple EC2 instances means managing and scaling servers, so it has more operational overhead than Lambda.
x.B: S3 events invoke a Lambda function as documents arrive. Lambda scales automatically, is highly available, and needs no servers. Results go into Aurora.
x.C: EBS Multi-Attach works only within a single AZ and with certain instance types, so it isn't highly available, and it needs server management.
x.D: ECS with the EC2 launch type still requires managing the underlying EC2 instances, which is more overhead.

x.A: FSx for Lustre is a high-performance file system for HPC on Linux, and its S3 integration lets you load on-premises data from S3 and write output files back to S3 for long-term storage.
x.B: FSx for Windows File Server is an SMB file system for Windows workloads, not for Linux HPC, and it isn't designed for HPC performance.
x.C: Glacier with EBS is not a high-performance shared file system for hundreds of instances.
x.D: An EBS volume can't be shared by hundreds of Spot Instances, and S3 with a VPC endpoint is not a file system.

x.A: ECR stores the images, ECS on Fargate runs the containers without servers to manage, and target tracking scales automatically. It is highly available with the least overhead.
x.B: ECS with the EC2 launch type still means provisioning and managing the EC2 container hosts.
x.C: Running your own repository and managing the instances and scaling yourself is a lot of operational work.
x.D: Baking the container into an AMI and scaling on CPU is a manual, heavy approach that doesn't use container orchestration.

x.A: Running Redis on a single EC2 instance means managing the server, and it is not highly available or built as a durable message queue.
x.B: Kinesis is for streaming data, and a failing record could block the processing of the remaining records in a shard. It is more complex than needed.
x.C: SQS holds messages for up to 14 days, so 2 days of processing is fine, and a dead-letter queue collects messages that fail so they don't block the others.
x.D: SNS pushes messages to subscribers but doesn't hold them for up to 2 days or provide a dead-letter queue by itself for slow processing.

x.A: The bucket policy can't use a WAF ARN as a principal, because WAF isn't what requests S3 content.
x.B: CloudFront doesn't forward requests to WAF as a separate step. WAF is associated with the distribution and evaluates requests there.
x.C: Security groups don't apply to S3, and CloudFront IP restrictions on S3 aren't done that way.
x.D: An OAI restricts the bucket so that only CloudFront can read it, and enabling AWS WAF on the distribution means all website traffic is inspected before content is served.

x.A: Presigned URLs give temporary access to private objects and do nothing to improve performance for millions of global viewers.
x.B: Replicating to every Region is costly and complex, and users would still need to be directed to the nearest bucket.
x.C: Geoproximity routing in Route 53 only affects DNS answers and doesn't cache or speed up content delivery.
x.D: CloudFront caches the static HTML pages at edge locations worldwide, which handles millions of views with low latency and takes load off S3.

x.A: Spot Instances can be interrupted, so using them exclusively would risk downtime, and the application must run continually.
x.B: Reserved Instances for the maximum capacity means paying for capacity that sits idle most of the time, given unpredictable and intermittent traffic.
x.C: Spot Instances for extra capacity could be interrupted at any time, which risks downtime for a workload that must continually process messages.
x.D: Reserved Instances cover the baseline at a discount, and On-Demand Instances handle spikes without interruption risk. It is the cost-effective choice that avoids downtime.

x.A: A network ACL controls subnet traffic. It cannot allow or deny AWS services or actions across accounts.
x.B: A security group controls network traffic to resources, not access to AWS services or actions.
x.C: Cross-account roles in each account would have to be created and maintained in every account, so there is no single point of control.
x.D: A service control policy in the root OU applies to all accounts below it and sets the maximum permissions. It is scalable and managed in one place.

x.A: Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, and you can't add an Inspector agent to an ALB.
x.B: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 and does not protect against DDoS attacks.
x.C: Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS detection and mitigation for resources such as the ALB.
x.D: GuardDuty detects threats and does not prevent DDoS attacks.

x.A: Security groups only allow rules by IP or security group, and can't filter by country.
x.B: The ALB's security group also works by IP range, so it can't restrict to a country without a long list of CIDRs.
x.C: AWS WAF has a geographic match rule that allows or blocks requests by country, and it can be associated with an ALB.
x.D: Network ACLs work with IP ranges only, and can't filter by country.

x.A: A single EC2 instance can't scale for holiday spikes and is a single point of failure.
x.B: API Gateway and Lambda scale automatically with demand, which is elastic for seasonal spikes, and you pay only for use.
x.C: Two EC2 instances behind an ALB are a fixed capacity and don't scale elastically.
x.D: API Gateway in front of one EC2 instance still limits capacity at the instance, so it doesn't scale.

x.A: A signed URL controls who can access a file in CloudFront and doesn't add extra encryption for sensitive form data.
x.B: A signed cookie also controls access to content, not the encryption of submitted data.
x.C: Field-level encryption encrypts specific sensitive fields at the edge, so they remain encrypted through the application stack until an authorized application with the private key decrypts them.
x.D: Setting the origin protocol policy to HTTPS only protects data in transit between CloudFront and the origin, but it doesn't add the extra protection the question asks for.

x.A: Global Accelerator speeds up traffic to servers but doesn't cache content, so it doesn't reduce the load on the origin.
x.B: CloudFront caches the same videos and images at edge locations around the world, which reduces the load on S3 and costs less than serving everything from the origin.
x.C: ElastiCache for Redis in front of web servers doesn't serve large media files to users worldwide, and it is expensive for this use.
x.D: ElastiCache for Memcached has the same issue and is not a media delivery cache for worldwide users.

x.A: Two Regions with Auto Scaling groups is more complex, and an Auto Scaling group works within a single Region, so this can't be done directly.
x.B: Spreading the Auto Scaling group across two AZs behind the ALB means the application keeps running if one AZ fails, without changes to the application.
x.C: A template ready to create instances in another Region is a manual recovery step, not high availability.
x.D: A round-robin configuration just spreads traffic, but all instances would still be in the same AZ, so an AZ failure would take them all down.

x.A: Provisioned concurrency makes more Lambda instances warm, which increases database connections, and a global database doesn't solve connection exhaustion.
x.B: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections, so a surge of Lambda invocations doesn't exhaust the database. Only the connection endpoint needs to change in the function.
x.C: A read replica in another Region doesn't help with open connections to the writer, and routing with query string parameters needs application changes.
x.D: Moving to DynamoDB would need a data migration and a major application rewrite.
